title: AI Cross-Checks May Flag H-1B Address Mismatches, Law Firm Warns
excerpt: Womble Bond Dickinson says AI-assisted reviews could surface inconsistencies between workers' AR-11 address filings and employers' worksite records — and that updating one does not fix the other.
body:
• US law firm Womble Bond Dickinson warns that AI-assisted checks could flag mismatches between an H-1B worker's residential address and the worksite in the employer's petition.
  • The classic trap: a worker files an AR-11 after moving, or an employer amends the petition for a worksite change — but not both, leaving the two records inconsistent.
  • Remote workers are most exposed: a home move can take the job outside the area covered by the existing labour condition application (LCA), requiring a new LCA and an amended petition.
  • What to do: report a home move to USCIS within 10 days via USCIS's change-of-address tool and tell your employer the same week — one filing never substitutes for the other.

US immigration authorities could increasingly use artificial intelligence tools to identify inconsistencies across immigration filings, according to a release issued by the law firm Womble Bond Dickinson — putting the accuracy of H-1B visa holders' records, and their employers', under a new kind of scrutiny.

The firm warns that AI-assisted checks could help officials compare information across earlier and current filings, surfacing discrepancies that manual review might miss. The most likely flashpoint is mundane: the gap between where a worker lives on paper and where the employer's petition says they work.

How a Mismatch Happens

One scenario highlighted by the firm involves an employer filing an amendment to an H-1B petition to reflect a change in worksite location after the employee has already submitted an AR-11 change-of-address notification to US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS). If the effective dates, addresses or other details across the two filings do not line up, an automated review can flag the record.

The reverse is just as risky. An employee who moves home but fails to file the required AR-11 leaves the government's records showing the old address; if the employer later updates worksite records or files a related petition, the comparison exposes the conflict.

Two Filings, Two Separate Duties

The mechanism matters because the two obligations are legally distinct. Form AR-11 — filed through the USCIS AR-11 page or the online change-of-address service — is the individual's duty to report a change of residential address, generally within 10 days of moving. An amended H-1B petition is the employer's duty when a material change in employment conditions occurs, including a change in the authorised worksite.

Completing one does not satisfy the other. A worker who dutifully files an AR-11 after a cross-town move may still be working at a location the petition does not cover; an employer who amends a petition has not discharged the worker's personal address-reporting duty.

Remote Work Raises the Stakes

The issue is sharpest for remote workers. An H-1B employee who relocates while keeping the same job may move outside the geographic area covered by the existing labour condition application. Depending on the circumstances, the firm notes, an amended petition and a new LCA may be necessary — even though nothing about the job itself changed.

Automated analysis also reaches backwards. Applications may no longer be assessed solely as individual submissions: officials comparing current filings against earlier petitions, employment verifications and address declarations could bring old discrepancies to light. Legal advisers recommend keeping copies of past filings and employer communications, and that sponsors audit records before submitting an extension or amendment.

What This Means for Indian Professionals

Indians constitute the largest share of H-1B holders, so consistency across address notifications, employment details and previous applications matters disproportionately for them. The firm is clear on one point: a flagged discrepancy does not, by itself, establish fraud or a violation. Dates, job locations and other particulars may differ because of administrative oversight, and the circumstances and supporting documents determine what a flag actually means.

A note on sourcing: this warning originates with a law firm's advisory, reported by Indian outlets on October 24, rather than with a USCIS announcement of a named AI programme. USCIS has not, in the reporting available, confirmed a specific AI cross-checking system — but the underlying compliance duties the firm describes, the 10-day AR-11 rule and the amended-petition requirement, are longstanding and verifiable on USCIS's own site.

What to Watch

Employers sponsoring H-1B workers are being advised to review how they record residential moves, worksite changes and petition amendments, and workers to notify employers promptly of any change. As AI-assisted analysis develops, the practical standard is simple: every address the government holds for you — home and worksite, old filing and new — should tell the same story.
